name: Belfry of Bruges
label: Belfry
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rozenhoedkaai' (4 web pages); placed at the stretch of Rozenhoedkaai nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/182727710: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Belfry' (28 m across).
notes: The 83 m medieval bell tower rising over the Markt.

text.description:
The Belfry of Bruges is the medieval bell tower that rises over the city centre, and it is one of the best-known sights in Bruges. It was added to the Markt around 1240, when the city was a major centre of the Flemish cloth trade. It stands 83 metres tall and leans about 87 centimetres to the east. It once reached 102 metres, but the wooden spire burned down in 1741 and was never replaced. The octagonal upper stage and the Gothic stone parapet make the top easy to recognise from far away. The tower has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1999.

The quay curves round a bend in the canal, and the brick guild houses are reflected in the water. The Belfry rises above the rooftops at the far end of the view, so the tower becomes the finishing touch to the scene. A few steps along the quay in either direction changes the angle, so try two or three spots. The quay is crowded for much of the day, so be patient and wait for a gap along the quay edge. If you want a different picture, Jan Van Eyckplein may show the Belfry across the canal after dark, though you should verify this view on arrival. The Markt gives a straight-on view of the tower over the guild gables, but it can be cluttered by scaffolding and café umbrellas, especially at night.
text.geographic_location: The Belfry stands on the Markt, the main square in the centre of Bruges, at the front of the old market hall. The Rozenhoedkaai viewpoint is a canal quay a short walk away.
text.directions_text: Start from the Markt, the main square, where the Belfry stands. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the canal bend, the guild houses and the reflections. Then try telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to bring the Belfry closer and fill more of the frame. The ultra-wide (0.5x) makes the tower look small and far away, so use it only if you want the whole quay in the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rozenhoedkaai (stone quay on the south side of the canal, near the bend where the Dijver meets the Groenerei; a few metres along the quay in either direction changes the angle). The canal bend with brick guild houses and their reflections in the water, with the Belfry rising above the roofs at the end of the view. On the stone quay on the south side of the canal, near the bend where the Dijver meets the Groenerei. From here the photo shows the canal bend, the brick guild houses and their reflections, with the tower closing the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the canal bend in the lower half so the reflections get plenty of space. Keep the tower near a vertical gridline so it looks upright. Move a few metres along the quay to shift the angle. For an alternative, Jan Van Eyckplein may give a canal view of the Belfry after dark (verify this view on arrival), and the Markt gives a straight-on vertical shot over the guild gables, though that view may be cluttered at certain times, especially at night.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the brick fronts to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky does not wash out and the Belfry keeps its detail. At blue hour, switch on night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a solid surface to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise and blue hour. The canal reflections work well at both times.

text.access_note: Rozenhoedkaai is a free public quay; climbing the Belfry itself is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Basilica of the Holy Blood
label: Holy Blood Basilica
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Burg' (6 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Burg' (way/158683638): middle (75 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/39262789: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilica of the Holy Blood' (57 m across).
notes: A small Romanesque chapel with a Gothic upper church on Burg.

text.description: The Basilica of the Holy Blood stands on Burg, a square in the historic centre of Bruges, right beside the Town Hall. It began in 1134 as a private chapel for the Count of Flanders, was finished by 1157, and became a minor basilica in 1923. It is really two chapels stacked together: a dark Romanesque lower chapel and a Gothic Revival upper chapel that holds the famous relic. Outside, the eye goes to the monumental staircase, built between 1529 and 1533 in late Gothic and Renaissance style. It was decided in 1832 to move it 4 metres back and rebuild it, and it is decorated with gilded bronze statues of rulers linked to Flanders. This makes the front a good phone subject: stone carving, gold details and the Town Hall next door all sit in one frame. The best photo is taken from across Burg, where you can fit the whole facade in and show how it sits with the buildings around it. The opposite corner of the square gives a slightly tighter, more layered look. Keep your photos to the outside. Photography is not allowed in the upper chapel where the relic is displayed. Visiting times for the interior vary between guides, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: On Burg square in the historic centre of Bruges, next to the Town Hall.
text.directions_text: Head for Burg, the square in the centre of Bruges beside the Town Hall. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot; head to Burg on foot and finish. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) from across the square for the whole facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough, and to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the statues on the staircase.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Burg (stand across the square and frame the facade; Chasing Hippoz suggests the opposite corner for compression). The Romanesque-Gothic facade of the basilica framed against the Town Hall and the rest of the square. From here the Romanesque-Gothic facade is framed against the Town Hall and the rest of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the building with the vertical lines so the facade does not lean. For a more compressed look, try the opposite corner of the square and zoom in a little. For a different angle, Gruuthuse Hof gives a side view of the basilica with the neighbouring medieval house fronts in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is washing out. Zooming in on the gilded statues is easier with the telephoto lens than by cropping later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 10:00 or after 17:00, when the square is quieter.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the open square, but the basilica is a place of worship with its own visiting rules and no photography in the upper chapel, so check the official site before you go.

name: Rozenhoedkaai
label: Rozenhoedkaai
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jan Van Eyckplein' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jan van Eyckplein' (way/126096386): middle (86 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W4332476 (Rozenhoedkaai): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The classic canal view with the Belfry rising behind the houses.

text.description:
Rozenhoedkaai is the stretch of quay where the canal bends and tall brick gabled houses rise straight out of the water, with the Belfry standing above the rooftops behind them. It is a very busy, popular spot with day visitors and boat trips, and the reason is easy to see on a phone screen: water, old brick, trees and a tall tower all fit in one frame. Because the quay is so busy, the calmest results come at sunrise or around blue hour, when the light is soft and the water is stiller.

For something a little different, this spot's suggested viewpoint is Jan Van Eyckplein, a short walk north along the canal. Guides describe it as quieter and far less photographed than the quay. It shows a calm canal stretch with guild buildings and streetlight reflections, and it works best after dark. One guide says it is largely empty after about 9 PM, which suits slow, steady night shots. A guide also suggests early morning if you want the square to yourself.

If you want the classic view as well, Nepomucenusbrug looks down the canal as it curves towards Rozenhoedkaai, with the quay facades, willows and the Belfry spire together. From the quay itself you can get low, close to the water, and let the gabled houses rise out of the reflection. Take a few frames from each place and compare them later.
text.geographic_location: Rozenhoedkaai lies on the canal in the centre of Bruges, with the Belfry rising above the roofs behind it. Jan Van Eyckplein, the suggested viewpoint, is on the same canal just to the north.
text.directions_text: From there Rozenhoedkaai is about 500 m (roughly 519 m) to the south along the canal. Look for the bend in the canal where the brick gabled houses come down to the water. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the canal and its reflections. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) on the quay itself when you want the full row of gables, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Belfry above the roofs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Jan Van Eyckplein (north of Rozenhoedkaai, along the canal). A quieter canal stretch with guild buildings and streetlight reflections, mainly useful after dark. Which is north of Rozenhoedkaai, along the canal. From the square you see a quieter canal stretch with guild buildings and streetlights reflected in the water. Rozenhoedkaai itself is to the south, so walk down the canal if you also want the close view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the canal edge up with a horizontal line so the buildings sit level. Include the streetlight reflections in the lower half of the frame and keep the buildings in the upper half. For the classic view, try Nepomucenusbrug, where the canal curves towards the quay with the Belfry spire above. On Rozenhoedkaai itself, crouch low so the gabled houses seem to rise out of the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or bridge rail to keep the phone steady. Tap on the brightest lit building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights don't burn out. In daylight, tap on the brick facade to set focus and exposure.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark for Jan Van Eyckplein, when guides say it is largely empty after about 9 PM. Sunrise and blue hour are the practical times for the quay, as it is very busy during the day.

text.access_note: Rozenhoedkaai is a free public space that is open at all times, though it is very busy during the day.

name: Groeningemuseum
label: Groeninge Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/11739150979: the OpenStreetMap point 'Groeningemuseum'.
notes: Fine-art museum with Flemish Primitives such as Jan van Eyck.

text.description: The Groeningemuseum is Bruges's municipal art museum, and it is the place to see Flemish and Belgian painting in one building. The collection runs across six centuries, from Jan van Eyck to Marcel Broodthaers. Early Netherlandish works are the headline, with Van Eyck's Madonna with Canon van der Paele (1436) among them. There are also pieces by Gerard David, Hugo van der Goes and Hieronymus Bosch's workshop, plus later Belgian symbolist and modernist work, including René Magritte. The museum stands on the site of the medieval Eekhout Abbey, which gives the spot some quiet history. For a phone photographer this is mostly an exterior stop: a record of the building you visited, taken at the museum. Take a few frames of the entrance and front, then a closer one of any signage or detail that catches your eye. If you go in, check the museum's own rules on photography before you take your phone out in the galleries. Many museums limit or ban photos of certain works. Give yourself a couple of minutes outside for a good set of pictures, then enjoy the paintings with your phone in your pocket.
text.geographic_location: The Groeningemuseum is in Bruges, Belgium, on the site of the medieval Eekhout Abbey.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. Use the map to reach the phone icon on the map at the museum. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the building. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough to fit the front in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the entrance or signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back a few paces if there is room, to fit more of the front in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's edges with them so the walls look straight. Hold the phone level and avoid tilting it upwards, which makes the walls lean inwards. Take one wide shot for context and one closer shot of the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright and the front looks dark. Do the opposite on a dull day if the walls look grey.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or overcast light is kind to a building front.

text.access_note: This is a municipal museum, so entry and photography rules inside may apply: check the official site before you go.

name: Church of Our Lady, Bruges
label: Church of Our Lady
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bonifaciusbrug' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bonifaciusbrug' (way/64610788): middle (6 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/92235134: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Church of Our Lady' (111 m across).
notes: Brick church with one of the tallest towers in the world, holding Michelangelo's Madonna.

text.description: The Church of Our Lady is a Roman Catholic church that dates mainly from the 13th, 14th and 15th centuries. Its brick tower is 115.6 metres high, which makes it the tallest structure in Bruges and the third tallest brickwork church tower in the world. That height is the reason it photographs so well. The picture is at its best when you stand on the Bonifaciusbrug and look back towards the church, with the water and garden lined up beneath the tower. The exterior is Gothic, with flying buttresses built in the 1270s and 80s. Inside, a chapel was made in 1482 for Lodewijk van Gruuthuse as his private place of worship, and the church holds a Michelangelo Madonna and Child. For a phone photo, the tower is so tall that you will usually want a portrait (upright) frame. Keep the bridge railing or a bit of ivy in the foreground, and the tower will look properly tall above them. The bridge is narrow and gets busy with tour groups from mid-morning, so go early and keep your phone steady while others pass. Inside the church, photography is allowed in the free nave but not in the museum section. Flash is usually banned.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Bruges, beside the canal and the Gruuthuse garden.
text.directions_text: Make for the Church of Our Lady in the centre of Bruges. The Bonifaciusbrug is on the north-east side of the church, about 1 minute on foot from it. Stand on the bridge and turn to face south-west, back towards the tower. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the canal, garden, ivy and tower all in one frame, as the bridge is narrow and you cannot step back. The default lens (1x) gives a calmer, less stretched view. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the brick tower with the water below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bonifaciusbrug (Stand on the bridge and face back toward the church, with the canal and garden in line with the tower). The brick Gothic tower rising above the canal, the Gruuthuse garden and ivy-covered walls in the foreground. Face south-west, back towards the church, so the canal and Gruuthuse garden run in a line with the tower. The ivy-covered walls fill the foreground, and the brick Gothic tower rises behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone upright so the whole tower fits in. Switch on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line, so it does not lean. Put the canal and garden in the lower third and the tower above them. If the bridge is too busy, the Minnewaterbrug (lake and Begijnhof in front, tower far off across the water) is an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the brick does not wash out. Take a few frames in a row, because people keep crossing the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mid-morning, when the sun clears the church roofline. Arrive early, because the bridge fills with tour groups from mid-morning onwards.

text.access_note: The view from the bridge is from a public bridge over the canal; for going inside the church or its museum section, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines on a phone can help keep a tall tower vertical in the frame.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) can fit more into the frame when you cannot step back, but it may stretch the edges of the picture.
The tower is visible from many corners of the old town.

name: St. Salvator's Cathedral
label: St. Salvator's
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Steenstraat' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Steenstraat nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/13261411: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint Salvator's Cathedral' (128 m across).
notes: The oldest parish church in Bruges, now its cathedral.

text.description:
St. Salvator's Cathedral is the Roman Catholic cathedral of Bruges, and its fortress-like west tower stands out above the surrounding rooftops. The tower is neo-Romanesque and 99 metres high. It was designed by the English architect Robert Chantrell after a fire brought the roof down in 1839, and its base is the oldest surviving part of the church, dating from the 12th century. The building was a parish church for centuries and only became a cathedral in 1834, which is why the tower was made taller and more imposing.

A good view of the tower is from Steenstraat, the shopping street the cathedral sits just off. The street's lines lead the eye towards the tower.

If you want a wider view, the open churchyard in front, Sint-Salvatorskerkhof, shows the brick Gothic facade with the tall tower. Take a few frames from each place and compare them. Inside, the cathedral is 101 metres long and holds tapestries made in Brussels in 1731. Check the rules for photography inside on the day.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Bruges, just off the shopping street Steenstraat, with the churchyard of Sint-Salvatorskerkhof in front of the cathedral. The Church of Our Lady is nearby.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Bruges, head on foot for Steenstraat, the shopping street the cathedral sits just off. Look up for the tall tower and walk towards it. The churchyard in front is the easiest place to step back and see more of the building. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the tower with the street leading up to it. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower's stonework and top. Try ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the street is too tight to fit the tower in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Steenstraat (stand along the street, looking toward the cathedral's south-west side where the tower rises). The neo-Romanesque west tower rising above the street-level houses, framed by the street's perspective. From here the neo-Romanesque west tower rises above the street-level houses, and the street's perspective frames it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the tower on one of the vertical lines, with the street running towards it. Hold the phone level, as tilting it upwards makes the tower lean. If you want a different view, Sint-Salvatorskerkhof, the churchyard in front, shows the full brick Gothic facade and the tower together.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky keeps its detail and the stone stays dark and rich. If people walk through the frame, try a Live Photo or take a quick burst and pick the cleanest shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning, when the shopping street is quieter, is likely to give you the clearest view. Mid-morning to afternoon is fine too, but expect people in the frame.

text.access_note: The street and churchyard are outdoors, but the cathedral is a place of worship, so dress modestly and check the official site before you go for visiting times and photography rules inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is likely to be quieter on the shopping street than later in the day.
Tilting a phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean inwards.
Visitors to a cathedral are generally expected to dress modestly.

name: Minnewater
label: Minnewater
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Minnewaterbrug' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Minnewaterbrug' (way/566957194): middle (48 m across); moved 20 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OSM W92158921 (Minnewater): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The 'Lake of Love', a calm basin with swans and a lock house.

text.description:
Minnewater is a lake and park in Bruges, and it is one of the calmest places on the map for a phone photo. The water is still enough to reflect the city's towers, and the Gunpowder Tower stands close by. Swans glide across the foreground, which gives you a ready-made subject for a postcard-style shot.

The best-regarded place to take the picture is the Minnewaterbrug, the pedestrian bridge over the lake. Guides call it the best photo spot on the water, because from up there you can frame the swans and the lake from above, with the park around them. Reviewers say both sides of the bridge give good views, so cross over and compare before you settle on one. If the bridge is busy, the Sashuis, the lock keeper's house beside the water, gives a closer and quieter view of the lake, framed by the park's greenery.

For a simple, balanced photo, put the water in the lower half of the frame and let the towers and trees fill the top. Switch on the gridlines to keep the horizon level. Then take one wide shot of the whole scene and one closer shot of the swans. Wait a moment for the surface to settle if a boat or a bird has stirred it, as the reflection is a large part of the picture.

The Minnewater is a place to stroll rather than rush, so allow time to walk round the water's edge and try a few angles.
text.geographic_location: Minnewater is a lake and park in Bruges, with the Gunpowder Tower nearby.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view of the water, swans and towers. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit more of the lake and park into the frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the swans or a tower reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Minnewaterbrug. The lake and park in the foreground with the Minnewater's water reflecting the city's towers and the Gunpowder Tower nearby. From here the photo shows the lake and park in the foreground, with the water reflecting the city's towers and the Gunpowder Tower nearby. Both sides of the footbridge give good views, so try each one.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level. Put the water in the lower third or half of the frame, with the towers and trees above, and a swan on or near one of the grid lines. For a quieter, closer view with the lock keeper's house and the park's greenery, walk to the Sashuis beside the water as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the water or the towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the reflections keep their colour. Hold still for a second after tapping, or try a Live Photo to catch a swan's movement and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon in spring or autumn gives soft light and usually fewer people. Golden hour, just before sunset, is another good choice.

text.access_note: The lake, park and bridge are open public space, but check the official site before you go if you plan to visit any buildings nearby.

name: Gruuthusemuseum
label: Gruuthuse Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/221477841: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gruuthusemuseum' (62 m across).
notes: The medieval palace of the lords of Gruuthuse.

text.description:
The Gruuthusemuseum is a museum of applied arts housed in the Gruuthuse, the medieval town house of Louis de Gruuthuse. The family took the name 'Van Gruuthuse' ('From the Gruit house') after the building, which was used to store and tax gruit. A wealthy Bruges family held the right to tax gruit and built a store for it, probably in the 13th century. In the early 15th century Jan IV van der Aa turned the building into a luxury family home. His son Louis added a second wing and, in 1472, a chapel that links the house to the neighbouring Church of Our Lady. That link between house and church is a good detail to look for in your photos.

The city of Bruges bought the house in 1875, and the architect Louis Delacenserie restored it between 1883 and 1895. The outside is partly original and partly rebuilt, so you are photographing a 19th-century vision of the Middle Ages as well as the real thing. Inside, the collection runs from the 15th to the 19th century and includes tapestries, bobbin lace, furniture and a painted terracotta bust of Charles V. There is also a small bronze bell thought to date from about 1245.

The building's outline is about 62 metres across, so a few different pictures help: one wide shot to show how it sits in the street, then closer shots of windows, architectural details and the chapel link towards the church. Take a little time to step back and check the edges of the frame.
text.geographic_location: The museum stands in central Bruges, right beside the Church of Our Lady, to which it is joined by the chapel Louis de Gruuthuse added in 1472.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from the Church of Our Lady, which is next to the museum. If you are coming from further across Bruges, go by taxi or hired scooter to the church and walk the last stretch. The phone icon on the map is at the centre of the museum, so you are there once you reach the building. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for windows, architectural details and the chapel link to the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back along the street until the whole building fits in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the horizontal edges of the roof and windows with them, so the building doesn't look tilted. Keep the phone level and don't tilt it upwards, which makes the walls lean inwards. Then take a second, tighter shot of a doorway or window for detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the front of the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the details keep their colour and the sky doesn't wash out. Indoors, check the signs and ask staff before using flash or taking photos.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or on a softly overcast day usually gives gentle light on the building and fewer people in the frame. Check the official site for opening and entry details before you go.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the public street. Check the official site for opening and entry details before you go.

name: Bruges City Hall
label: City Hall
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Burg' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Burg' (way/158683638): middle (75 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/825379781: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'City Hall' (76 m across).
notes: One of the oldest Gothic town halls in the Low Countries.

text.description:
Bruges City Hall (the Stadhuis) is the grand Gothic building on Burg Square, in the old centre of Bruges. It was built between 1376 and 1421 and is one of the oldest city halls in the former Burgundian Netherlands. Its stone facade, with rows of tall windows set in repeating niches, small turrets and a crenellated top, inspired the city halls of Brussels, Ghent, Leuven and Oudenaarde. The statues on the front were destroyed at the time of the French Revolution and have been renewed since, and the left-hand door was moved in 1766 to make the front look more balanced.

It photographs well because the facade is detailed but sits on an open square, so you can fill the frame with it. From there the facade fills the picture, and the Basilica of the Holy Blood shows at the left corner in early light. Take one wide shot of the whole front, then step in and use the telephoto lens for the niches, turrets and carved details. A second option is Blinde Ezelstraat, an alley where you get a compressed first view of the facade as you step out into the square. The outside views cost nothing, but the interior is a separate visit, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The City Hall stands on Burg Square in the centre of Bruges, on the site of the former fortified castle. The Basilica of the Holy Blood is visible at the left corner from the viewpoint.
text.directions_text: Head for Burg Square in the centre of Bruges. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the turrets, niches and carved details. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close and cannot fit the front in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Burg (south-central edge of the square, facing the City Hall facade). The Gothic Stadhuis facade filling the frame, with the Basilica of the Holy Blood visible at the left corner in early light. From here the Gothic front fills the frame, and the Basilica of the Holy Blood shows at the left corner in early light.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the edges of the facade up with them so the building does not lean. Keep the whole front in the frame with the basilica corner on the left. For a more dramatic alternative, try Blinde Ezelstraat, where the facade appears compressed as you step out of the alley into the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone with both hands and keep your elbows tucked in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The hour after sunrise, when the square is usually emptier, so fewer people end up in your shot. The hour before sunset is also worth trying.

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from the open public square, but the interior is a separate paid visit that may restrict flash and tripods, so check the official site before you go.

name: Markt (Market Square)
label: Markt Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Markt' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Markt' (relation/5301046): middle (188 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5301046: 'Belfry', the best-known feature inside 'Markt' (189 m across).
notes: The main square, lined with guildhall-style gabled houses.

text.description:
The Markt is the central square of Bruges, and it is the easiest place in the city to understand where you are. The Belfry stands on the south side, one of the city's most famous landmarks, and the stepped-gable guild houses and café terraces line the other edges. The square covers about a hectare, and since its renovation in 1995–96 it has been mostly traffic-free, so you can stand back and take in the whole scene without cars in the way.

The Belfry works as a strong vertical anchor in a wide frame, which is why the view facing it is the classic shot. In the middle of the square is a statue of Jan Breydel and Pieter de Coninck, who fought at the Battle of the Golden Spurs in 1302. It was unveiled in 1887 and makes a handy foreground. A diagonal angle lets you add the guild houses and café terraces to the tower.

The square has been a gathering place since the 10th century, with its first international fair around 1200. Early morning gives the cleanest compositions. After dark the Belfry is lit and the cobbles are quieter.

For a different view, turn to face the Gothic civic facade and the colourful houses across the open cobbles. If you want a bird's-eye view of the whole square, the Belfort van Brugge looks straight down on it.
text.geographic_location: The Markt is in the heart of Bruges' city centre, with the Belfry on its south side and the Provincial Court building on its east side.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Bruges and head for the Markt, the main square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the Belfry, the guild houses and the cobbles into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, then use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the Belfry's upper tower or the statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Markt (from the square's centre, facing the Belfry). The Belfry rises over the square, framed by the stepped-gable guild houses that line it. From here the tower rises over the square, framed by the stepped-gable guild houses on either side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the Belfry on a vertical line so the tower stays upright. Keep the phone level and don't tilt it upwards, or the tower will lean. For a variation, step to one side for a diagonal angle that adds the guild houses and café terraces. You could also turn to the Gothic civic facade across the cobbles for a second shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Belfry to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and the tower keep their detail. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body for a few seconds.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning for clean compositions with few people; after dark for an illuminated Belfry and empty cobblestones.

text.access_note: The Markt is an open public square; if you want to go up the Belfry or enter any building, check the official site before you go.

name: Burg Square
label: Burg Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Blinde Ezelstraat' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Blinde Ezelstraat nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/100769581: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Burg' (53 m long).
notes: The historic civic square with the town hall and the Basilica.

text.description: Burg is one of the main squares of Bruges and one of the oldest parts of the city centre. Its name is Middle Dutch for "fortress", and it began as a walled stronghold where the Roman road met the Reie canal. Steen Castle, a residence of the Counts of Flanders, once stood on the western side. The square roughly doubled in size to around 1.1 hectares when Saint Donatian's Cathedral was demolished in 1799. Today it is framed by the Gothic City Hall, the Basilica of the Holy Blood and several other historic buildings. That mix of facades is why it photographs so well. The best approach is to come in through Blinde Ezelstraat, the narrow arched passage beside the City Hall. The alley is tight and shaded, and then the square opens up in front of you, so the City Hall facade looks framed and a little dramatic. Once you are in the square, step back for a wide shot of the Basilica and its statues against the open space. The small Gruuthuse Hof courtyard beside the Basilica gives a different angle, but check on arrival that it is open. Keep to exterior views of the Basilica, as photography of the relic and the upper chapel inside is not allowed. The square is usually busiest around midday and calmer before 10:00 and after 17:00.
text.geographic_location: Burg sits in the historic heart of Bruges, beside the City Hall and the Basilica of the Holy Blood, a short walk from the Markt. The Rozenhoedkaai canal view is a short walk to the south.
text.directions_text: There are no station or tram stops listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Bruges (the Markt area) and walk in. Head for the arched passage of Blinde Ezelstraat on the south side of the City Hall and walk through it into the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the arch and the whole City Hall facade together. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and switch to 2x or more to pick out the Basilica's statues and facade details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Blinde Ezelstraat (the arched passage on the south side of the City Hall, where you emerge into the square). The Gothic City Hall facade framed by the archway as you step out of the alley into the square. In the arched passage on the south side of the City Hall, where you emerge into the square. From here the Gothic City Hall facade is framed by the archway as you step out of the alley.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the arch around the facade so the dark edges act as a frame. Keep the phone level so the building does not lean. Once in the square, take a second wide shot of the Basilica of the Holy Blood and its statues set against the width of the square. The small Gruuthuse Hof courtyard is another option for a different angle on the Basilica.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright stonework keeps its detail against the dark arch. Take a few frames at 0.5x and 1x so you can choose later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The first hour after sunrise is best, and the square is also calmer before 10:00 and after 17:00. Midday is usually the busiest.

text.access_note: The square and the passage are open public space, but check the official site before you go for the Basilica, City Hall and the Gruuthuse Hof courtyard, as access and photography rules inside may vary.
claims_not_in_sources: A narrow, shaded passage is a place where the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps fit the whole facade in.
A dark arch against a bright stone facade can cause the facade to overexpose, so lowering the exposure slider helps.
The Gruuthuse Hof courtyard is beside the Basilica and may not be open at all times.

name: Princely Beguinage Ten Wijngaerde
label: Beguinage
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wijngaardbrug' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Wijngaardbrug' (way/116029940): middle (11 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/957833481: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Begijnhof Ten Wijngaerde' (327 m across).
notes: A peaceful whitewashed convent courtyard with daffodils in spring.

text.description:
The Princely Beguinage Ten Wijngaerde is the only preserved beguinage in Bruges. It was founded around 1244 and now works as a Benedictine convent. No beguines live there any more. Inside are about thirty white-painted houses from the late 16th to 18th centuries, mostly arranged around a central yard, with a Gothic church among them. You reach the main entrance over the three-arched stone Wijngaard Bridge, and the arched gateway at the far end dates from 1776.

It photographs well because everything is simple and clean: pale walls, a stone bridge, water and trees. The classic frame is taken from the bridge itself, looking towards the gate, with the whitewashed houses rising behind it. This is the view most often shared. If you go through the gate, the white gabled houses wrap around the green lawn, with the entrance arch in the background. A second gate leads to the Sas House, which is a handy alternative frame with the canal edge and white houses.

This is a working convent, so keep your voice down and stay off the grass where signs ask. Do not point your phone into residents' windows or doorways. Photography in the courtyard is allowed, but one guide says drones are not permitted and another says commercial photography needs permission. Go very early in the morning if you can, before the tour groups arrive.
text.geographic_location: In the south of Bruges, reached over the Wijngaard Bridge. The beguinage sits on a green, tree-lined site beside the water.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Bruges, head south to the Wijngaard Bridge. From there the middle of the beguinage is to the west, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view of the gate and houses. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) inside the courtyard, where the lawn and gabled houses need a wider frame. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the arch of the gateway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Wijngaardbrug (from the bridge, looking toward the gate). The three-arched stone bridge leading to the 1776 white arched gateway, with the whitewashed houses rising behind it. The photo shows the line of the three-arched stone bridge leading to the white arched gateway of 1776, with the whitewashed houses rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the gateway in the centre, keeping the vertical walls straight. Let the bridge lead the eye towards the arch. For a second option, go into the courtyard for the white gabled houses around the lawn, with the entrance arch in the background. The Sas House side of the site is another alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white walls to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so they stay bright but not washed out. Hold the phone steady with both hands and keep your elbows tucked in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Very early morning, before the tour groups arrive.

text.access_note: The grounds are a working convent with a museum house, so check the official site before you go for access rules, and keep quiet and respect any signs.

name: Halve Maan Brewery
label: Halve Maan Brewery
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Walplein' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM N3509874031 (Halve Maan): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic family brewery of Brugse Zot beer.

text.description:
The Halve Maan Brewery is a brown-brick brewery building on Walplein in Bruges, and it is easy to recognise in a photo. Its golden half-moon logo sits on the facade, and a small arched entrance is where groups go in and out. That mix of warm brick, gold lettering and a neat arch gives you a simple, tidy picture even if you only have a minute.

The best view of the outside is from the open part of Walplein, facing the brewery front across from the restaurants. Stand back far enough to get the whole facade in, then take a second, closer shot of the logo and the arched doorway. People coming and going through the entrance add a bit of life to the closer picture, though you may need to wait a moment for a clear gap.

The brewery's own address is Walplein 26. If you want to go inside or take a tour, check the official site before you go. The views from the roof and tower are part of the paid tour and show the city rather than the brewery, so this spot is about the building from the square. Keep the phone level, use the gridlines to keep the vertical lines of the brickwork straight, and take a few frames so you have a choice later.
text.geographic_location: In the old centre of Bruges, on the square called Walplein, with the brewery front facing the restaurants opposite.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Walplein in the centre of Bruges. The brewery sits on the square, while the best viewpoint is the open part of Walplein facing the brewery front, so step back into the square to see the whole building. Look for the brown-brick front with the golden half-moon logo. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole facade. Switch to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the logo and the arched entrance. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you cannot step back far enough, and keep the building centred so the edges do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the best view, step back into the open part of Walplein and face the brewery front across from the restaurants. From there you can see the brown-brick facade, the golden half-moon logo and the small arched entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the building with the vertical lines. Take one wide shot with the whole facade, then a closer one with the logo and the arch. Wait for a gap in the passing groups if you want a clean entrance. A canal-side spot nearby may give the facade with water in the foreground, but it is not marked on this map.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick wall to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the gold logo looks washed out. Check the picture for tilted vertical lines before you move on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight works best for the colour of the brick and the gold logo. Earlier in the day is likely to be calmer if you want fewer people at the entrance.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but entry to the brewery and its tours may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Sint-Janshuismolen
label: St. John's House Mill
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kruisvest' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kruisvest' (way/171979353): edge nearest the subject (1010 m across).
pin_note: Position from OSM W218084313 (Sint Janshuismolen): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: One of the surviving windmills on the Kruisvest ramparts.

text.description:
Sint-Janshuismolen is a windmill on the rampart edge of Bruges, and from the grassy slope below it the whole mill fits in one frame. The sails and the body of the mill are tall and clear-cut, so they make a strong shape against the sky. The grass around it gives you room to step back and fit the whole thing into one frame.

The best everyday view is from Kruisvest, on the grassy slope below the rampart, facing the mill. From there the sails and the body sit together in a single shot, with sky behind them. Visitors also mention the path up to the mills, which gives closer views, and the lawns of the neighbouring park, which are a pleasant place to stand and look at it.

If you want a second picture, try the Sint-Janshuis Mill mound. It gives a quieter, wider view over the rooftops of the St Anne's Quarter, with the mill at the edge of the frame instead of in the middle.

Opening times for going inside can vary, and the mill may be closed in winter. You may only be able to photograph it from outside then, which still works well. Check before you go if you hope to visit the inside.
text.geographic_location: Sint-Janshuismolen stands on the rampart edge of Bruges, next to the Kruisvest park, close to the St Anne's Quarter.
text.directions_text: Start from the St Anne's Quarter or the Kruisvest park and head for the mill. Walk down onto the grassy slope below the rampart and turn to face the mill. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the grassy slope, where the whole mill fits in the frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you move closer along the path and the sails no longer fit. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the sails.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Kruisvest (grassy slope below the rampart, facing the mill). The whole mill framed against the sky, with the sails and body fitting in one frame. On the grassy slope below the rampart, facing the mill. From here the whole mill fits in one frame, with the sails and body against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the mill on one of the vertical lines. Leave some sky above the sails so they are not cut off. Keep the phone level so the tower does not lean. For a different view, the Sint-Janshuis Mill mound gives a wider shot over the St Anne's Quarter rooftops, with the mill at the edge of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mill to focus. Slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so it stays blue and the sails keep their detail. If you are standing with the sun in front of you, tap on the mill's body and lower the exposure.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening is the generally recommended time, ideally with the sun behind you so the sky behind the mill is blue. Note that from where you stand the mill lies to the south-west, so the low afternoon or evening sun will be in front of you there. In that case tap on the mill and lower the exposure, as described above. If you want the sun behind you from this spot, a morning visit is the better choice.

text.access_note: The slope and park around the mill are open public space, but going inside the mill is separate and may be ticketed or seasonal, so check the official site before you go.

name: Bonifaciusbrug
label: Bonifacius Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bonifaciusbrug' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W64610788 (Bonifaciusbrug): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: A small stone bridge by the Dijver canal, among the most romantic corners of Bruges.

text.description:
Bonifaciusbrug is a small, narrow pedestrian bridge over one of Bruges' canals, and photo guides call the view from the bridge the classic angle. The reason is the view along the water. Standing on the bridge and facing north, you look up the canal between old brick facades, with the tower of the Church of Our Lady rising behind as a backdrop. The canal leads the eye straight to the tower, which gives you a simple, balanced picture without any fuss.

The bridge has steps at both ends and is not wheelchair accessible, so it suits a short, relaxed stop on foot. It is also quite small, so take your photo, then step aside so others can have their turn. The bridge also looks good from either bank of the canal. If you would like a picture of the bridge itself, Arentshof gives the view from the water's edge, with the Church of Our Lady tower behind it. That is the angle most often cited as the best photograph of the bridge.

Guides say it gets crowded from mid-morning, once tour groups arrive, so an early start works best. Late evening is another option one guide suggests. Keep your phone steady against the parapet if you can, and check the lens for smudges before you shoot.
text.geographic_location: In Bruges, on a canal with the tower of the Church of Our Lady rising behind the view to the north.
text.directions_text: Follow the phone icon on the map to the bridge. Once you are there, the tower of the Church of Our Lady is visible to the north, rising behind the canal. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which suits the canal, the facades and the tower together. Try the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want to include more of the bridge and the buildings beside you.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the water runs away between the old brick facades, with the tower of the Church of Our Lady behind. For a different view, try Arentshof, where you can photograph the bridge from the water's edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the canal in the centre so it leads the eye to the tower. Keep the phone level so the brick facades stay straight. Include a little of the water in the foreground. Move to one side of the deck so you are not in other visitors' way. For a picture of the bridge itself, walk to Arentshof and shoot from the water's edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its detail and the brickwork stays rich. Switch on Live Photos if you want a moment of movement on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the tour groups arrive around mid-morning. One guide also suggests late evening.

text.access_note: The bridge is a narrow pedestrian bridge with steps at both ends and is not wheelchair accessible.
claims_not_in_sources: Arentshof is within a short walk of the bridge.
A telephoto lens brings a distant tower closer and makes it look larger in the frame.

name: Old St. John's Hospital
label: St. John's Hospital
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/465040917: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Site Oud Sint-Jan' (300 m across).
notes: A medieval hospital that now houses works by Hans Memling.

text.description:
Old St. John's Hospital (Sint-Janshospitaal) sits right beside the Church of Our Lady and holds some of the oldest surviving hospital buildings in Europe. It was founded in the mid-12th century as a place where sick pilgrims and travellers were cared for, and a monastery and convent were added later. In the 19th century more building produced a hospital with eight wards around a central building. The old hospital was nearly demolished in the 1860s, but interest from Gothic Revival supporters, especially Englishmen living in the city, saved it, and the new hospital was built alongside instead. It stopped working as a hospital in 1977 and the city took over the buildings. Part of the complex is now the Hans Memling museum. The square inside the site was named after Eleonora Verbeke, an 18th-century nun at the hospital, in 2020.

It photographs well because several centuries of building stand close together, so you can pick out a roofline, a doorway or a run of old walls and get a good picture without needing a wide view. The phone icon on the map is in the middle of the site, so you can turn around and shoot in several directions. Take a few frames with different framing: one wide shot to show the setting, then closer shots of details such as windows, brickwork and gables. Keep your phone level, as buildings lean noticeably if you tilt it upwards.
text.geographic_location: In Bruges, next to the Church of Our Lady. The hospital grounds include the square named after Eleonora Verbeke.
text.directions_text: Head for the Church of Our Lady in Bruges; the old hospital is right next to it. Walk the rest of the way from there. The phone icon on the map is in the middle of the hospital site, so once you are inside the grounds you are already there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for most views. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you can step back only a little, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out gables, windows and other details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The subject is at this same spot, so you are photographing the old buildings around you. Turn slowly and look for the best angle on the walls and rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up vertical walls with the vertical lines so the buildings do not appear to lean. Use an archway or doorway as a natural frame for a second shot. Take one wide picture to show how the buildings relate to each other, then a few close ones of the details.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick or stonework to set focus, then use the exposure slider to pull the brightness down slightly if the sky looks washed out. Avoid the 0.5x lens for close-up details, as it stretches the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day or later in the afternoon, when there are usually fewer people in the grounds and the light is softer. Overcast days work well for even colour on the brickwork.

text.access_note: The grounds and the Hans Memling museum may have ticketed or restricted areas, so check the official site before you go.

Overcast light gives even colour on brickwork.
Buildings appear to lean if the phone is tilted upwards.
Parts of the grounds and the museum may be ticketed or have restricted access.

name: Jan van Eyckplein
label: Jan van Eyckplein
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Koningsbrug' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Koningsbrug' (way/305523123): middle (10 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/126096386: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jan van Eyckplein' (86 m across).
notes: The old harbour square with the Poortersloge and a statue of the painter.

text.description: Jan van Eyckplein is a small square beside a canal in Bruges, named after the Northern Renaissance painter Jan van Eyck. It sits where Academiestraat, the Spiegelrei and Spanjaardstraat meet. That makes it a good place to photograph the water, the gabled guild-house fronts and the Gothic tower of the Poortersloge together. The square itself is pleasant, but the best picture comes from a little way off. Stand on the Koningsbrug, the bridge over the Spiegelrei, and look back towards the square. From there the tower and its reflection in the canal fit into one frame, which is why guides single this bridge out as the best vantage point. The still water does much of the work, so a calm day gives the cleanest reflection. Early morning or soft, overcast light is recommended, and blue hour after sunset also suits the scene. Keep your phone level so the tall buildings don't lean, and watch for passers-by or boats crossing the reflection. If you want something different, look south from the bridge for a wide view of the guild facades. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, because the same spot gives you both a wide scene and a tighter tower-and-water shot.
text.geographic_location: Jan van Eyckplein is in the old centre of Bruges, in West Flanders, where Academiestraat, the Spiegelrei and Spanjaardstraat meet beside the canal.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so walk in from the old centre of Bruges to the Spiegelrei canal. The square is then about 170 m to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the tower, the square and the canal reflection into one frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the guild facades looking south. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the tower alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Koningsbrug (bridge over the Spiegelrei, looking back west toward the square). The square and the Poortersloge tower framed together, with the canal reflection in the same frame. Look back towards the square to the south-west. From here you see the square and the Poortersloge tower framed together, with the canal reflection in the same shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the water line on the lower third, so the reflection fills the bottom of the picture and the tower rises above it. Hold the phone level to keep the buildings upright. For a second view, walk along the Spiegelrei canal bank for gabled facades reflected in the water. You can also try the square itself, where the tower can be shot against the sky from the side rather than head-on.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. In the evening or at blue hour, use night mode and rest your elbows on the bridge parapet to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or an overcast day, when the light is soft and the water is calm. Blue hour after sunset is also recommended by several guides.

text.access_note: No ticket is needed for the viewpoint.

name: St. James's Church
label: St. James's Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sint-Jakobsplein' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Sint-Jakobsplein' (way/300654966): middle (22 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/135907202: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St. James's Church' (86 m across).
notes: A Gothic church with rich interior art, in the old merchant quarter.

text.description:
St. James's Church (Sint-Jakobskerk) is a Catholic church in Bruges, and its plain brick walls and heavy tower make a good subject for a phone. The building dates from around 1240. It was enlarged considerably in 1459, when Bruges was growing rich, and the Duke of Burgundy was among its patrons. The inside was remodelled in the Baroque style in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. Some people call it St. Jacob's, but that name is a mix-up: Flemish uses one word for both James and Jacob.

From outside, the appeal is the solid brick and the squat crossing tower, which rises above the roofline. The tone is warm and the shapes are simple, so the church works well as a straightforward, uncluttered picture. Start on the square where the church stands, Sint-Jakobsplein, and take a wide view first. Then look at the smaller details: brickwork, windows and the lines of the roof. If you have time, walk round the building, because the side streets give different angles on the walls and tower. Keep your phone level, or the tall walls will lean inwards in the picture. Gridlines help with this. If you plan to go inside, bear in mind that opening details may have changed, and that interior photography is limited to no flash.
text.geographic_location: St. James's Church stands on Sint-Jakobsplein in Bruges. The square is where the church has its official address.
text.directions_text: Make your way on foot to Sint-Jakobsplein in Bruges. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the brick walls and tower together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the church is too big to fit from where you are. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the top of the tower and the brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Sint-Jakobsplein. The church's brick exterior and heavy crossing tower, framed from the square where the church is located. From there the church lies to the north-east, and you can see its brick exterior and heavy crossing tower from the square it stands on.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the tower with a vertical grid line so the walls look straight. Include a little of the square in the foreground to show how big the church is. Then walk around the building and try the walls and tower from the side streets for a different angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the brick keeps its colour and the sky doesn't wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight, such as morning or late afternoon, tends to suit brick best. In harsh midday sun the shadows on the walls can be strong.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the square. Opening details for the inside may have changed, so check before you go, and if you photograph inside, do not use flash.
